title: Behavioral Finance
body:
**Behavioral finance** studies how real investors depart from the rational agent that classical
finance assumes. Its claim is that the departures are systematic and predictable, so they
persist where random noise would average away.

The classical model assumes investors process information rationally and that mispricings are
arbitraged away quickly. Behavioral finance keeps the model as an approximation and documents
where it fails, which is why the field is evidence-driven.

The findings the report draws on:

```
loss aversion       a loss hurts more than an equivalent gain pleases,
                    which makes investors hold losers and sell winners
overconfidence      investors overestimate their own information, which
                    produces excessive trading and worse returns
anchoring           a purchase price becomes a reference point with no
                    bearing on what the asset is worth now
limits to arbitrage a mispricing can persist because correcting it requires
                    capital and the ability to stay solvent while wrong
```

The last one carries the most weight. Classical finance assumes mispricing is corrected
quickly, and in practice correcting it means betting against a crowd for an unknown period,
which is why sentiment can move a price and keep it there.

This is the same subject [[ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE]] treats formally in
[[Rational Agent]] and [[Expected Utility]], where the utility function is concave in
money and that concavity is risk aversion. Behavioral finance is the empirical study of where
actual behaviour departs from that model, and [[Cognitive Bias]] in
[[INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY AND SOCIETY]] covers the same failures outside a
financial setting.
